new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress usually falls on the second syllable of the word (Di'tal, Ki'ta); the article a and the future marker a are unstressed clitics in the utterance; disyllabic reduplicated forms are usually stressed on the first syllable ('bobo, 'gege); and connected speech has syllable timing with a light rhythmic stress on every other syllable. The intonation section adds that 'the intonation system does not seem to be as important as the stress' and 'the stress pattern is the most important'.
new_statements.secondary_stress: 'In normal speech there is a definite syllable timing with a light stress which seems to take place on every other syllable' (1974 p. 18 = 1962 p. 6): an alternating light rhythmic stress, not described further.
new_statements.exceptions: Disyllabic reduplicated forms are usually stressed on the initial syllable ('bobo 'to look', 'gege 'crooked'); the article a and future-tense marker a are never stressed; the object pronoun ia is stressed after velar nasals (ng) but otherwise 'the preceding consonant takes the stress' (examples 'Da(t) 'vung 'ia, 'Pat a 'ka'p ia, 'Iau tar 'ki'ta ia); the rule is hedged as 'usually' and as 'tendencies of the accent system'.
new_statements.identity_note: The Tolai Language Course describes Tolai = Kuanua (ISO ksd) of the Gazelle Peninsula; its tapes use 'a central dialect (Matupit)' and its dialect report (1962 ed. p. 97) says dialect differences (Rabaul, Vunadidir, Rapitok, Raluana, Vunamami, Livuan, Matupit) are 'slight and regular' and concern prenasalization, flapped vs trilled r and final-consonant loss, not stress. Bley 1912 'Nordgazellen-Sprache' is the same language (not opened).

B. rá pia. Beim Sprechen werden die Wörter nicht scharf von einander getrennt. Die Endbuchstaben eines Wortes werden meistens mit den Anfangsbuchstaben des folgenden verbunden. Euphonie, s. Lekt. 40. [p. 7-8 examples as printed:] kilála (Zeit) ... káukau (Morgenfrühe), ... lúluai (Herr), ... tarái oder taréi (Männer), vuái oder vuéi (Frucht, F. tragen), kunái oder kunéi (Gras). oi z. B. in: borói (Schwein), ou z. B. in: kóukou (Süßkartoffel).
new_statements.translation: II. Pronunciation. Syllables can be long (—) or short (⏑). Both long and short syllables can be stressed. The accent can also fall on a monosyllabic word, e.g. rá pia. In speaking, the words are not sharply separated from one another; the final letters of a word are mostly joined to the initial letters of the following one. Euphony, see Lesson 40. [Examples pp. 7-8 with the acute marking the stressed vowel: kilála 'time', káukau 'early morning', lúluai 'chief', tarái/taréi 'men', vuái/vuéi 'fruit', kunái/kunéi 'grass', borói 'pig', kóukou 'sweet potato'.]

new_statements.relation_note: What differs: the catalog codes Kuanua as fixed-STRICT second-syllable stress (StressTyp2; Franklin/Kerr 1974 sec. 5.4 'Stress usually occurs on the second syllable', 5.5 'Reduplicated forms (two syllable) are usually stressed syllable initial'). Bley 1912 gives no placement rule at all and instead marks the accent lexically on each word; his marked vocabulary has many initial-stressed NON-reduplicated di- and trisyllables (káva 'gebären', tági 'weinen', líbur 'spazieren gehen', árig 'bitten', pápalum 'arbeiten', bólo, móno, díma, dóko, ébar, qáramut, qárere, qátuqat) beside the second-syllable ones, and stem-bound stress on the third syllable in var-prefixed reduplications (varvakíta etc.)…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Bley states NO placement rule. His only explicit statement (p. 8): syllables are long or short; stress may fall on long and on short syllables alike (i.e. stress is not tied to syllable length); a monosyllabic word can carry the accent within the phrase (rá pia); words are run together in speech. Instead of a rule he marks the stressed vowel with an acute, word by word, in the pronunciation examples, throughout Lektion 26 and on the headwords of the kanakisch-deutsch Woerterverzeichnis. The marked forms (eye-read from the page scan) show stress on the second syllable in many words (kilála, borói, tarái, kunái, vuái p.7-8; ipúk, igít, vakó, toróm, diép, iróp, viók, kukúl, kakál, kikíp, mumút, tutún, mamál, kakáp, kakáo, loálop pp.103-104; dovót, elép, etép, enána, qalúm, qelég, qoból, qamáta, qanáo, qalíaka p.194) but on the first syllable in many others, reduplicated and not (káukau, kóukou, lúluai p.7; káva, tági, pápalum, váogo, árig, tútumu, pípil p.103; líbur, káo, kópag p.104; túrtur, kíki, kúlkul, mútmut, bólo, móno, kánkan, gága, búkabuka p.105; díma, dóko, dúdu, ébar, éleve, qáki, qéqe, qíqi, qáramut, qárere, qátuqat p.194), and on the third in prefixed/reduplicated forms where it stays on the stem (varvarúbu, varvakíta, varvatóvo, varvavúl, torátorom p.104; diradíra, qalaqála, qeqelúl p.194). Fully reduplicated monosyllables go both ways (túrtur, kíki, kúlkul, mútmut vs tutút, papá, enén, kaká, alál, akák, apáp, urúr, irír p.105). So the book treats the accent as something to be learned per word, with a visible second-syllable tendency, not as fixed.
new_statements.secondary_stress: nothing stated; only one acute per word is printed
new_statements.exceptions: none stated as such (no rule is given); the explicit remarks are that stress is independent of syllable length and that monosyllables can bear the phrase accent (rá pia). Dialect notes on pp. 8 and 177 concern consonants and euphonic vowels (Blanchebucht, Weberhafen-Vuatom-Nodup), not accent.
new_statements.identity_note: Bley describes the 'Nordgazellen-Sprache', i.e. the Tolai/Kuanua of the north-eastern Gazelle Peninsula (Catholic mission standard, Vunapope/St. Paul; orthography protocol Rabaul 10 Nov 1909), with side remarks on the Blanchebucht and Weberhafen(-Vuatom-Nodup) dialects (consonants, euphonic vowels), none about accent. Same language as the catalog's Kuanua entry.

readall_conflicts: Franklin, Kerr & Beaumont 1974 (the catalog's basis) state a second-syllable rule hedged with 'usually', initial stress in disyllabic reduplications, and an alternating light rhythmic stress; StressTyp2/the catalog hardened this into fixed-strict second-syllable stress. Bley 1912, the oldest and fullest description (Rakunai/Vunapope mission standard, 'Nordgazellen-Sprache'), states no placement rule, says only that both long and short syllables can be stressed and that monosyllables can take the accent, and marks stress per word with an acute throughout Lektion 26 and the kanakisch-deutsch dictionary; those marks fall on the second syllable in many words but on the first in many non-reduplicated words (káva, tági, líbur, árig, pápalum, bólo, móno, díma, dóko, ébar, qáramut, qárere, qátuqat) and on the stem (third syllable) in var-prefixed reduplications. The two sources therefore agree on a second-syllable tendency and on initial stress in many reduplications, but Bley's data contradict the 'strict' part of the catalog's classification and point to lexically specified stress with a second-syllable preference. Mosel 1980 and the SIL OPD (held by the project from earlier passes) are silent on stress.
